title: Allergic rhinitis
overallBottomLine:
• Empiric treatment of patients with classic symptoms is appropriate.
  • Treatment with intranasal steroids and nonsedating antihistamines is sufficient for most patients.
  • Intranasal steroids are also effective in treating ocular symptoms associated with allergic rhinitis.
  • Allergy testing is recommended for patients with severe symptoms, for patients who have failed other therapy, or for patients whose diagnosis is unclear.
  • Subcutaneous and sublingual immunotherapy are burdensome and have some risk, but can produce long-lasting remission of symptoms.

parts.label: Definition
parts.html: Allergic rhinitis (AR) is characterized by IgE-mediated inflammation of the mucus membranes lining the nasal passages in a sensitized individual, leading to the typical symptoms of sneezing, nasal obstruction, nasal itching, and mucus discharge, all of which are reversible spontaneously or with treatment.

parts.label: Prevalence
parts.html:
• US prevalence is estimated from 80 to 300 cases per 1000 adults. 27 28
  • In an unselected population of 2320 individuals at a public fair in Belgium in 2012, the overall prevalence of AR was 31%. 34 Prevalence rates of sensitization by skin prick test were about 25% each for grass pollen and house dust mite and 13% for tree mix. Sensitization to at least one of the allergens was present in 40% of the subjects. Symptomatic sensitization was somewhat lower at 18% for grass, 17% for dust mites, and 10% for trees.
  • In a study of children aged 3 to 5 years in Beijing in 2012, almost half (48%) of parents reported AR, but only 31% of those could be confirmed by skin prick testing. 35
  • A systematic review of pediatric AR showed an overall prevalence of self-reported current AR of 18% and lifetime AR of 20%; physician-diagnosed AR was 10.5%. 92

parts.label: Economic impact
parts.html: • Economic impact of AR is $1.2 billion to $4.5 billion per year in direct medical costs and up to $7.7 billion when including indirect costs.

parts.label: Other impact
parts.html:
• AR is the sixth most common chronic illness.
  • There is an association between otitis media with effusion and AR (aOR = 3.4; 95% CI, 1.3-9.0). 36
  • AR has been shown to affect examination performance of teenagers. 26
  • In a multicenter observational cross-sectional study of 990 primary care patients with AR, ocular symptoms and, to a lesser degree, nasal obstruction and pruritus have a significant impact on quality of life. 37
  • AR is associated with disordered sleep. 87 60 61
  • AR with atopy is related to worsening of asthma. 62
  • Using genome-wide association studies including 66,645 patients with allergic diseases and 12,281 patients with dementia, authors found that allergic rhinitis may be causally associated with an increased risk of Alzheimer’s disease (OR 1.2, 95% CI 1.0-1.4) and vascular dementia (OR 1.3, 95% CI 1.03-1.6). 95

parts.label: Causes of the condition
parts.html:
• Exposure to an allergen in a sensitized patient leads to AR symptoms.
  • Data on frequencies of sensitization to each of the many allergens in large populations are not available. 29

parts.label: Pathophysiology
parts.html:
• An inhaled trigger allergen is bound by specific IgE antibodies to IgE receptors on mast cells of respiratory mucosa.
  • Mast cells degranulate, releasing chemical mediators of inflammation. These mediators synthesize further mediators and chemicals that attract other inflammatory cells causing a delayed phase of inflammation.
  • Research is focusing on the role of microRNAs, a class of single-stranded RNA molecules that post-transcriptionally silence gene expression and appear to have important roles in regulating allergic inflammation. 63

parts.label: Bottom-line
parts.html:
• Observational studies have found an association between breastfeeding for at least 4 months and a reduction in the risk of atopic disease 25; however, a single large RCT did not substantiate this finding. 2
  • Maternal dietary restrictions during pregnancy do not seem to have a major role in preventing atopic disease. 25
  • Parental cleaning of pacifiers with their own mouth decreased the likelihood of allergy sensitization, asthma, and eczema. 59 In this study, 74% of the 184 infants followed used a pacifier during the first 6 months of life.
  • Postponing introduction of solid food (nuts, fish, or eggs) and cow’s milk does not decrease incidence of AR. 24 4
  • Early-life supplementation with probiotics did not protect against AR, asthma, eczema, or food allergy at age 5 years. 64
  • Dust mite-proof covers for beds and pillows do not decrease atopic disease in the first 2 years of life. 23

parts.label: Bottom-line
parts.html:
• The diagnosis of AR is based on typical symptoms, examination, and response to a therapeutic trial of medication.
  • If allergy testing is required because of severe symptoms, failure to respond to therapy, or uncertainty of diagnosis, skin prick test is the test of choice. 1 22
  • Measurement of allergen-specific IgE may be used when skin testing is impractical. 29

parts.label: Diagnostic criteria
parts.html:
• AR is classically divided into seasonal and perennial.
  • About one quarter of patients with AR can be sub-classified as having local AR (LAR). 65 LAR involves only a nasal allergic response, including local IgE, in the absence of systemic atopy. Patients with “systemic” AR have positive skin prick test responses and serum IgE levels to inhalant allergens.
  • A World Health Organization (WHO) guideline divides AR into intermittent (<4 days/week or <4 weeks/year) or persistent disease (>4 days/week and >4 weeks/year). 29
  • The WHO also classifies AR by its impact on daily life as mild, moderate, or severe based on abnormal sleep or impairment of daily activities, including sport and leisure activities, work, and school.

parts.label: Using the history and physical
parts.html:
• AR typically develops before age 20 years and often in individuals with a family history of atopy. Interestingly, having siblings or being a second- or later-born child was associated with a decreased risk of current allergic rhinitis (RR 0.9, 95% CI 0.8-0.95 and RR 0.8, 95% CI 0.7-0.9, respectively). 96
  • AR is usually diagnosed clinically. Symptoms include runny nose; nasal congestion; sneezing; and itchy mouth, nose, or eyes.
  • Since rhinorrhea is common to all rhinitis, symptoms of itchy nose, sneezing, itchy, watery eyes, and response to a specific allergen are most useful in differentiating allergic rhinitis. 21
  • Supporting physical findings include "boggy" appearing, pale, swollen nasal mucose, clear discharge, and allergic "shiners".
  • However, symptoms and even nasal endoscopy findings do not reliably predict allergic rhinitis, as documented by skin prick testing in a referral population. 66 This may be due in part to the lack of systemic response in patients with LAR.
  • In a study of 194 patients with LAR, conjunctivitis was present in about half and asthma was present in 18.8%. 65
  • In a longitudinal study of children aged 1 through 4 years and again at age 7 years, positive parental responses to having either hayfever or ocular symptoms had the highest specificity (84% and 69%, respectively) and percent agreement (74% and 68%) with physician-diagnosed AR. 38
  • Engorgement of nasal mucosa can lead to eustachian tube dysfunction, cough, and sinus pressure. More severe AR can be associated with fatigue and headache.

parts.label: Selecting diagnostic tests
parts.html:
• Skin prick testing is generally less sensitive but more specific than intradermal testing; it is also safer. 22 A practical guide to skin prick testing in patients with allergy is available. 33
  • Allergen-specific IgE antibody testing (radioallergosorbent test [RAST]) is most useful if percutaneous testing is not practical or if the patient is taking interfering medications. A RAST is highly specific but less sensitive than skin testing and is less useful for food, venom, or drug allergies.
  • Many symptom-free people have positive skin prick or IgE antibodies. 29
  • Serum total IgE is not specific and should not be used to diagnose AR.
  • Blood or nasal eosinophilia suggests allergies; neutrophils suggest infection.
  • Some patients with AR also have bronchial hyperreactivity. Exhaled nitric oxide (FeNO) strongly correlates with response to bronchodilator testing and could be useful as a test of bronchial reversibility in children with AR or asthma. 39 Exercise challenge does not appear useful in testing for airway hyperresponsiveness in patients with rhinitis symptoms alone. 40
  • The Self Assessment of Allergic Rhinitis and Asthma questionnaire may assist clinicians in identifying asthma in patients with AR. 67

  • A visual analogue scale may be useful for monitoring progress. 68

parts.label: Bottom-line
parts.html:
• A stepwise, tailored approach to treatment is indicated, depending on severity of disease, patient preference, and cost and efficacy of drugs (see Figure 1).
  • Nasal steroids are more effective than oral antihistamines for nasal symptoms and equally effective for eye symptoms. 19 20 20
  • Second-generation or “non-sedating” antihistamines may cause less sedation than first-generation antihistamines such as diphenhydramine, but the difference may not be clinically relevant. 18

parts.label: Drug therapy
parts.html:
• Since first-line treatments are relatively free of side effects, it is appropriate to have a low treatment threshold for empiric treatment. 21 Consider beginning with intranasal treatments.
  • Steroids
  • Nasal steroids are more effective than oral antihistamines for nasal symptoms and equally effective for eye symptoms. 19 20 Once daily nasal beclomethasone dipropionate use at 320 μg/day is effective and does not appear to suppress the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal-axis. 41 69
  • Monotherapy with nasal steroids is recommended for initial therapy, rather than combining it with oral antihistamines. 81
  • Short courses of systemic steroids may relieve AR. 16 However, the substantial risks of long-term treatment usually outweigh the benefits. 88
  • Antihistamines
  • In an RCT with 610 patients with moderate to severe seasonal AR, the intranasal antihistamine azelastine was comparable to intranasal fluticasone in reduction in total nasal symptom score and reduced score from baseline. 53
  • Authors of a meta-analysis of 3 short-term (14-day) RCTs for AR found intranasal combination azelastine (a second-generation, selective, histamine antagonist) and fluticasone propionate superior to either intranasal drug alone, based on the nasal symptom score. 42
  • Second-generation or “non-sedating” oral antihistamines may cause less sedation than first-generation antihistamines such as diphenhydramine, but the difference may not be clinically relevant. 18
  • Decongestants
  • Intranasal decongestants are effective but should not be used for more than 10 days to decrease the risk of rhinitis medicamentosa. 17 Oral decongestants relieve nasal congestion resistant to other medications but may cause bothersome side effects.
  • Other agents
  • A mast cell stabilizer (cromolyn) for nasal use is considerably less effective than intranasal steroids and is prescribed 4 times a day but is quite safe.
  • Intranasal ipratropium (Atrovent) may be useful to decrease the rhinorrhea of AR.
  • Leukotriene-receptor antagonists (Montelukast, Zafirlukast) given orally are minimally effective for AR, but may be helpful as add-on therapy. 15 76 81
  • Combination omalizumab, a monoclonal anti-IgE antibody, and allergen immunotherapy was found to be more effective than allergen immunotherapy alone for improvements in symptom severity score and rescue medication daily means score with fewer episodes of severe systemic adverse effects based on a meta-analysis of 11 RCTs including 901 patients. 97
  • An open-label (non-deceptive) placebo was more effective than usual care. 93

parts.label: Surgical treatment
parts.html:
• Transnasal resection of the posterior nasal nerve (TRPN), submucous inferior turbinectomy, and turbinoplasty with resection of peripheral branches of the posterior nasal nerve are surgical procedures used for drug therapy-resistant, intractable AR.
  • Based on a review of case studies of 1677 patients with refractory AR, of whom 510 had combined chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps, both endoscopic vidian neurectomy and vidian-branch neurectomy were effective in improving patient-reported outcome measures including quality of life and improvement in nasal symptom severity in both short- and longer-term studies. 98 The endoscopic approach was more likely to cause dry eyes and palatal numbness, but there were no other serious complications with either procedure.
  • In a case series, investigators noted similar short-term symptom improvement for 11 patients undergoing TRPN combined with turbinoplasty and peripheral nerve resection and 13 patients undergoing submucous inferior turbinectomy with peripheral nerve resection alone. 43
  • In an RCT of 60 patients with persistent AR, extraturbinal microdebrider-assisted inferior turbinoplasty (MAIT) performed better with respect to rhinorrhea, sneezing, and nasal itching at 1 year than intraterbinal MAIT. 70

parts.label: Complementary/alternative therapy
parts.html:
• Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of 65 RCTs involving 3,634 participants concluded that gastrointestinal microbiome supplementation in the form of probiotics, prebiotics, and synbiotics was of benefit for patients with allergic rhinitis over the control group on symptom improvement, overall nasal condition, overall quality of life and medication score. 99
  • Homeopathic immunotherapy for dust mite allergen is not effective. 14
  • Based on methodologically poor quality data, butterbur 4 times daily, may be as effective as antihistamines. 13
  • Chinese herbal medicine may have beneficial effects in patients with AR based on a metanalysis of a series of small studies at high risk of bias. 32 In another meta-analysis of 7 papers, Chinese Herbal medicine reduced recurrence of AR. 100
  • In an RCT of acupuncture vs. sham acupuncture in 21 patients with AR, those randomized to active treatment demonstrated statistically significant improvements in disease-specific quality of life and antihistamine use measures after 8 weeks of treatment. However, the clinical significance of these differences is not clear. 44
  • In another RCT with 238 subjects with AR, acupuncture reduced total nasal symptom scores more than sham acupuncture or a waitlist group. 54 Both active and sham acupuncture were effective in producing a significant change in the total non-nasal symptom scores compared with the waitlist group.
  • Helminth therapy involves deliberately introducing helminths, on the theory that this antigen exposure reduces symptoms or incidence of auto-immune diseases such as asthma. Authors of a Cochrane review of 2 small single center placebo-controlled RCTs of percutaneous or oral helminth administration found a reduction in days during grass pollen season when participants needed rescue medication for their AR. However, they found no differences in AR symptoms, percentage of well days, lung function measures, or quality of life scores. 45 Reported side effects of helminth therapy were primarily gastrointestinal including moderate or severe abdominal pain, flatulence, and diarrhea.
  • Herbal steam baths (30 minutes/day, 3 times a week for 4 weeks) were no more effective than plain steam baths. 82

parts.label: Other treatment
parts.html:
• Immunotherapy
  • Subcutaneous immunotherapy (SCIT) is effective and may cause permanent cessation of symptoms, 12 especially with single-allergen regimens. 71 However, immunotherapy is expensive and burdensome, often requiring years of therapy, and it carries a small risk of life-threatening anaphylaxis. 29 Allergy immunotherapy appears to reduce health care costs in patients with newly diagnosed AR. 55
  • Sublingual immunotherapy (SLIT) also appears effective in alleviating AR symptoms. 10 46 101 In one study, the most common treatment-related adverse events with SLIT to ragweed were localized pruritus and nasal and throat irritation. 47 A study with tree pollen allergies showed good efficacy with mild to moderate local side effects. 85 A systematic review and meta-analysis for grass pollen SLIT was less favorable. Side effects were reported by 60% of patients, including anaphylaxis that required epinephrine. 77 Individual studies showed sublingual allergen tablets are modestly effective for patients with confirmed allergy to grass pollen 11 48 and house dust mites 83. SLIT may not offer long-lasting relief after discontinuation. 79 SLIT for ragweed and grass pollens is currently available in the U.S.
  • Authors of a meta-analysis of 6 trials found moderate evidence supporting SCIT over SLIT for nasal and/or eye symptom reduction. 56 However, authors of a recent review found the two treatments comparable with respect to efficacy and side effects and recommend that decisions about which treatment be based on local availability and patient preference. 80 Practice guidelines exist for SLIT and SCIT. 94
  • Nasal Irrigation
  • Saline nasal irrigation performed regularly over a limited period (up to 7 weeks) for patients with AR has a positive effect on nasal symptoms (28% improvement), a reduction in medicine consumption (62%), and improved quality of life (28%). 49 In another trial, however, of three different nasal saline irrigations, only patients using buffered isotonic saline with mild alkalinity had improved nasal symptoms and none of the solutions improved mucociliary function or nasal patency. 50 Saline irrigation is more effective than saline spray for patients with nasal symptoms, including AR. 3 A squeeze bottle may work better than a bulb syringe. 89
  • Authors of a Cochrane review concluded that saline irrigation may reduce patient-reported disease severity compared with no saline irrigation at up to three months in both adults and children with AR, based on low or very-low quality evidence. 90 There were no reported side effects.
  • Environmental Control
  • Interventions designed to decrease dust mite exposure (acaricides, HEPA filters, bedroom-based environmental control procedures) may be of some benefit for highly sensitized patients. Isolated use of impermeable bedding is unlikely to benefit. 30
  • Removal of carpets and humidity control decreases house dust mite load and may alleviate symptoms in sensitive individuals. 9
  • A bedroom high-efficiency particulate air filter, however, did not decrease allergy symptoms in an RCT of 90 patients with pollen allergy. 86
  • Other Treatments
  • Nasal filters appeared effective in reducing nasal symptoms. 31 78
  • Phototherapy and intranasal phototherapy appear effective in treating symptoms of AR. 72 73

parts.label: Bottom-line
parts.html:
• One study reported that after 8 years of following patients with AR, a small percent spontaneously resolved (12% of patients allergic to pollen, 19% to animals, and 38% to dust mites). Decreasing sensitization correlated with reduced IgE levels. 8
  • At 5-year follow-up of 194 patient with LAR, 26.2% had worsening of rhinitis persistence and severity. 65 Systemic atopy developed in 6.8%, similar to the control group at 4.5%.
  • Long-term immunotherapy may completely resolve or significantly reduce symptoms making further treatment unnecessary. 17
  • Rhinitis symptoms tend to become less pronounced over time in elderly patients.

parts.label: Pregnancy
parts.html:
• Pregnancy-induced hormones may produce a clear rhinorrhea that can be mistakenly identified as AR.
  • Topical therapies including intranasal steroids and oral antihistamines (chlorpheniramine, loratadine and cetirizine) are widely considered safe in pregnancy. Specific safety data other than reports from widespread use are not available.

parts.label: Infants and children
parts.html:
• Cetirizine causes sedation (slower reaction times and decreased performance) in children but does not cause drowsiness (subjective feeling of being tired). 7
  • In one RCT, cetirizine syrup was more effective in relieving symptoms than placebo in 6-11-year-olds. Loratadine was not effective. 84
  • School performance was not affected by either diphenhydramine or loratadine. 6
  • Nasal steroids are effective but may cause a small but statistically significant decrease in growth velocity in children. 5 75 74
  • There is strong evidence supporting precoseasonal tablet and drop grass pollen SLIT for allergic rhinitis in children. 57 Moderate evidence supports use of SLIT for house dust mite alone and dual house dust must and grass pollen, although the former study is of low quality. Based on 3 studies, there is little evidence to support use of SCIT over SLIT for improving rhinitis symptoms or medication usage in children; local reactions were frequent with both treatments. 58
  • Authors of a meta-analysis of separate studies including 4122 children with AR treated with SLIT and 1852 treated with SCIT found comparable outcomes on improved symptom scores, medication scores, new sensitizations, and development of asthma between the SLIT and SCIT groups; however, the SLIT group had a significantly lower incidence of treatment-related adverse effects. 102
  • In an RCT including 52 children with AR, a nursing intervention for home environment modification reduced the number of triggers in the home environment, but had no significant effect on symptom control or quality of life. 103

figures.title: Algorithm for Evaluation and Treatment of Allergic Rhinitis

cells.html: Suspected allergic rhinitis (history and exam). Avoid allergens and irritants.
Second-generation antihistamine, oral or intranasal, as needed
Daily intranasal corticosteroid; if severe, consider steroid–antihistamine combination spray
Step up: intranasal steroid plus intranasal antihistamine. Rhinorrhea: add ipratropium spray. Severe congestion: oxymetazoline for 3 days or less.
Skin prick or serum specific IgE testing, or refer to allergist
Targeted allergen avoidance; consider immunotherapy (subcutaneous or sublingual tablets)
Continue treatment; step down when allergen exposure decreases
Reconsider diagnosis: nonallergic or drug-induced rhinitis, rhinosinusitis, structural causes, local allergic rhinitis. Consider ENT referral.

notes: Adding an oral antihistamine to an intranasal steroid adds little benefit.
Montelukast only if other options fail or are not tolerated (FDA boxed warning).
Avoid first-generation antihistamines and systemic or depot corticosteroids.
